title: Dietary reference values for sodium
authors: EFSA Panel on Nutrition, Novel Foods and Food Allergens (NDA), Turck D, Castenmiller J, de Henauw S, Hirsch-Ernst KI, Kearney J, et al.
funder: European Food Safety Authority, on request from the European Commission (question number EFSA-Q-2011-01224).
authorConflicts: Declarations of interest of panel members are held by EFSA; not read.
result: Sodium chloride is the main constituent of table salt; 1 g of sodium chloride provides 0.4 g of sodium and 0.6 g of chloride. In healthy people almost all dietary sodium is absorbed, along most of the small and large intestine; apical co-transporters couple sodium entry to the uptake of solutes, the basolateral Na+/K+-ATPase exchanges three intracellular Na+ for two extracellular K+, net sodium and water absorption occurs in the distal ileum and colon, and distal absorption responds to aldosterone. Renin is released from the juxtaglomerular apparatus in response to reduced afferent arteriolar pressure, increased sympathetic activity and decreased distal tubular NaCl; renin hydrolyses angiotensinogen to angiotensin I, which angiotensin-converting enzyme converts to angiotensin II; angiotensin II stimulates proximal sodium reabsorption, arteriolar constriction and adrenal aldosterone release; aldosterone stimulates sodium recovery in exchange for potassium in distal tubule, collecting ducts and distal colon. Genotypes with increased ENaC function cause volume expansion, hypertension and hypokalaemia (e.g. Liddle's syndrome). A sodium intake of 2.0 g/day is considered safe and adequate for adults, including pregnant and lactating women.
